chapter_theme: Speech can't be judged apart from its hearers. One must read the assembly and adjust: shine among the bright, stay silent or whitewashed among the dull, step carefully among the great, and never spill nectar where it can't be received.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: speak only after knowing the assembly (711-712), the fault of not doing so (713), a summary of how to behave (714), conduct before superiors (715-716), before equals (717-718), and before inferiors (719-720).

711.reading: Those whose purity lies in knowing the body of words should speak after knowing the assembly and examining the matter.
711.nuance: Pope's 'pure in heart' gives the wrong impression. For Parimelazhagar, தூய்மை here is selection: discarding what doesn't suit and keeping what does. It's a purity of diction, not of character, though the verse doesn't rule out more.

712.reading: Those with the goodness of knowing how words work should discern the opening, understand clearly, and then speak.

positions.position: இடை is the moment: when the assembly is willing to hear.
இடை is the fault: think about what wrong a word could bring.

713.reading: Those who undertake to speak without knowing the assembly don't know the kinds of speech, and have no ability at all.
713.nuance: A strong claim about what speech is. Parimelazhagar's reason is that kinds of speech follow from kinds of hearers' understanding, so if you don't know the hearer, you don't know the words.

714.reading: Before the bright be bright; before the empty, take on the colour of pure white plaster.
714.nuance: The verse plays on வெளி, the blank and white. Parimelazhagar connects it to வெளிறு, wood without heart, and says one should appear even whiter than they are so they will respect you. It's unusually candid advice to feign emptiness; the commentators don't soften it.

715.reading: The best of all things called good is the restraint of not speaking first among elders.
715.nuance: Parimelazhagar notes the exact limit: only speaking first is forbidden, so speaking with them or after them remains allowed. Manakkudavar extends முதுவர் beyond age to austerity, family and learning, and this matters because the verse gives only the one word.

716.reading: A slip before those who have taken in and understood wide learning is like faltering from one's footing on the path.

positions.position: The path is the path to liberation: it is like an ascetic falling away, with loss of fruit and scorn as well.
It is simply someone who is on a path of life and loses his standing, and is scorned.
positions.quote: ஒரு நெறியின்கண் நின்றார் அந்நிலைமை குலைந்தாற்போல் இகழப்படும்

717.reading: The learning of those who have studied and understood shines where people can examine words faultlessly.
717.nuance: Learning needs a qualified audience to appear at all. Manakkudavar puts this as a limit: only the learned can tell how good learning is.

positions.position: Those with the skill to examine words are the assembly: speak in such a gathering.
positions.quote: வழுப்படாமல் சொற்களை ஆராய்தல் வல்லார் அவைக்கண் சொல்லின்

positions.position: They are the speakers themselves: learning shows in those who choose flawless words.

718.reading: Speaking before those with understanding is like pouring water on a bed where the crop is already growing.
718.nuance: The image could suggest redundancy, since the crop grows anyway. Parimelazhagar takes the opposite point: what would grow by itself grows all the more, and what grows is the speaker's own learning.

719.reading: Those able to speak well and effectively in a good assembly should not, even by forgetting, speak in a mean one.
719.nuance: Parimelazhagar's reason is double: the good assembly scorns you for not knowing your audience, and the mean one for not grasping the matter. பொச்சாந்தும், 'even by forgetting', treats it as a slip one must be on guard against.

720.reading: Holding forth before those who aren't of one's own group is like nectar spilled in a dirty yard.
720.nuance: The verse's division is தங்கணத்தார் அல்லார், those not of one's group, which is a matter of fit and not explicitly of worth. Pope's 'alien herd' and 'inferior rank' sharpen it. Parimelazhagar sees the waste as twofold: those who would know it as deathless food never get it, and the yard gains nothing.

links.note: Two poured liquids in three verses: water on a growing bed and nectar in a yard. Nectar is much more precious than water and yet the outcome is reversed. What decides the value of speech is the ground that takes it, not the substance.

Both use the phrase கோட்டி கொளல், holding forth in company. 401 faults the speaker for lacking learning, and 720 faults the hearers for lacking fitness. Together they give both ways a speech can fail.

The adjacent chapter says fearless speech in assembly is rarer than courage in battle. 715 says that the best of all good things is holding back among elders. The chapters are a pair and Parimelazhagar reconciles them with precision: only speaking first is restrained.

source_issues: 711: The verse reads அவையறிநது, a typographical error for அவையறிந்து.
712: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (தௌ¢ந்து for தெளிந்து).
714: Parimelazhagar's text has an encoding error (ஔÿபுள்ளிÿளியாரவைக்) and reads கதையின் where the verse needs சுதையின், and it ends with a stray ') ---'.
719: The verse's second line reads நன்குசலச், a typographical error for நன்கு செலச் (as in Parimelazhagar's lemma).
720: Manakkudavar's commentary is marked as not aligned. Parimelazhagar's text places the label விளக்கம் in the middle of the explanation.
